Cost-Minimization of Endometrial Biopsy Strategies for Lynch Syndrome
Surveillance

**Précis:** Combining endometrial biopsy with an already-scheduled
colonoscopy costs less than standalone office biopsy or operative dilation
and curettage across a range of assumptions and locations.

## Abstract

**Objective:** To estimate and compare the health-system costs of three
strategies for endometrial cancer surveillance in women with Lynch syndrome:
standalone office endometrial biopsy, operative dilation and curettage
(D&C), and endometrial biopsy performed during an already-scheduled
surveillance colonoscopy.

**Methods:** We built a decision-analytic, cost-minimization model from a
U.S. health-system/payer perspective, using Medicare-anchored allowed
amounts (2026 U.S. dollars). Each strategy was modeled as an initial
sampling attempt that either succeeds or fails and escalates to operative
D&C; the combined-biopsy strategy included only costs incremental to the
already-planned colonoscopy. Clinical probabilities were drawn preferentially
from Lynch-syndrome-specific literature. We conducted deterministic and
probabilistic sensitivity analyses (1,000 Monte Carlo draws), a threshold
analysis, a budget-impact analysis, a geographic sensitivity analysis using
real Medicare Geographic Practice Cost Indices and hospital wage indices
across four localities, and two supplementary clinical-outcome sensitivity
analyses testing the model's assumption of equivalent diagnostic
effectiveness across strategies.

**Results:** In the base case, combined biopsy cost an estimated $506.11 per
patient, compared with $749.18 for standalone office biopsy and $3,839.81
for operative D&C. Combined biopsy was $243.06 (32.4%) less expensive than
standalone office biopsy and was cost-saving in 91.4% of probabilistic
sensitivity analysis draws. Combined biopsy remained the least expensive
strategy across all four geographic localities tested, with its advantage
over standalone office biopsy widening from $195.62 in a low-cost locality
to $333.44 in a high-cost locality. Clinical-outcome sensitivity analysis
found combined biopsy carried substantially lower exposure to
D&C-rescue-driven adverse events than standalone office biopsy (mean 0.36
vs 2.48 events per 1,000 patients).

**Conclusion:** [DRAFT -- directly supported by data, no "further research
needed" language, per journal requirement] Endometrial biopsy performed
during an already-scheduled surveillance colonoscopy costs substantially
less than standalone office biopsy or operative dilation and curettage for
Lynch syndrome surveillance, and this advantage is robust to parameter
uncertainty and practice location.

Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by pathogenic
variants in the DNA mismatch repair genes that confers a substantially
elevated lifetime risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer, with
endometrial cancer risk approaching that of colorectal cancer in affected
women and, in some carriers, presenting before a colorectal cancer
diagnosis. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network recommends
gynecologic surveillance with endometrial biopsy every 1-2 years beginning
at age 30-35, alongside interval colonoscopy (NCCN category 2A).^16^ This
guideline specifies timing and eligibility, not delivery method. Office
endometrial biopsy
is the standard sampling method but is frequently painful, requires a
dedicated clinic visit distinct from the surveillance colonoscopy, and can
fail to obtain an adequate specimen.

Performing endometrial biopsy during an already-scheduled surveillance
colonoscopy, under the sedation the colonoscopy already requires, has been
described as feasible and better tolerated than standalone office biopsy in
single-institution cohorts. What has not been established is whether this
combined approach is also less costly to the health system than the two
existing alternatives -- standalone office biopsy or operative dilation and
curettage (D&C) -- once the full cost of an escalation to D&C after a
failed sampling attempt is accounted for in each strategy. We built a
decision-analytic, cost-minimization model to estimate and compare the
health-system costs of these three strategies, and to test, rather than
assume, whether the model's cost conclusion depends on the assumption of
equivalent diagnostic effectiveness across strategies, on Medicare-derived
parameter uncertainty, or on practice location.

## Methods

We conducted a cost-minimization analysis comparing three strategies for
endometrial cancer surveillance in adult women with Lynch syndrome who are
candidates for gynecologic surveillance and have an already-scheduled
surveillance colonoscopy: standalone office endometrial biopsy, operative
dilation and curettage (D&C), and endometrial biopsy performed during that
colonoscopy (combined biopsy). Transvaginal ultrasound was not modeled as a
fourth comparator: NCCN's own guideline states that transvaginal ultrasound
has not been shown to have sufficient sensitivity or specificity to support
a screening recommendation in this population, in contrast to endometrial
biopsy.^16^

Age, genotype, menopausal status, and prior
biopsy history were not modeled separately; the model represents a single
surveillance episode rather than a specific patient subgroup. No
prespecified health economic analysis plan was registered before the
analysis began; complete parameter-level sourcing is provided as
supplementary material.

The analysis took a U.S. healthcare-sector perspective. Healthcare resources
were valued primarily using Medicare allowed amounts (the Physician Fee
Schedule and the Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
Public Use Files),^6^ supplemented by published resource-cost estimates for
services not separately reimbursed, such as incremental procedure-room and
anesthesia time and scheduling-coordination labor. Patient time,
transportation, lost productivity, and other nonmedical costs were excluded.
All costs are reported in 2026 U.S. dollars; costs originally reported in an
earlier year were inflation-adjusted using the Bureau of Labor Statistics
Consumer Price Index for Medical Care. The analytic horizon was a single
endometrial-surveillance episode, beginning with the initial sampling
strategy and extending through any rescue D&C required after an
unsuccessful initial attempt; costs or consequences beyond resolution of
that episode were not included. Because the horizon was less than one year,
costs were not discounted.

Total expected cost per patient was the primary outcome, selected because
the decision this model addresses -- which sampling strategy a program
should adopt -- is, in the base case, a cost-minimization question: a
cost-minimization design assumes equivalent clinical effectiveness across
strategies, specifically that an adequate endometrial specimen provides
equivalent diagnostic information regardless of which strategy obtained it.
We did not extend the base case to a full cost-effectiveness or
cost-utility analysis (no quality-adjusted life-year axis, willingness-to-pay
threshold, or efficiency frontier). Instead, we selected two secondary
outcomes -- D&C-related adverse-event exposure and delayed-neoplasia
probability -- specifically to test, rather than merely assume, this
equivalence (described below). Both secondary outcomes are reported as
event counts per 1,000 patients; neither was converted to a utility,
quality-adjusted life-year, or monetary value, so no outcome valuation
step was required for them.

Each strategy was modeled as a one-step decision tree: an initial sampling
attempt, which either succeeds or fails and escalates to operative D&C. D&C
itself was modeled as a deterministic reference arm with no escalation
branch of its own in the base case; its cost also includes a partial
expected cost for uterine perforation, restricted to the one management
pathway (diagnostic laparoscopy) with a cost fully traceable to current
Medicare payment data,^6,7^ weighted by that pathway's observed probability
in an independent cohort study of postperforation management.^14^ See
Discussion for what this deliberately excludes. The combined-biopsy arm was modeled
under an incremental-cost principle: because the patient is assumed to be
undergoing the surveillance colonoscopy regardless of whether biopsy is
added, no colonoscopy base cost, gastroenterology professional fee, or
baseline procedural sedation cost was charged to this arm; only costs
incremental to the already-planned colonoscopy were included.

Clinical probabilities were drawn preferentially from Lynch-syndrome-specific
literature. The office biopsy failure probability was pooled from three
studies confirmed genuinely specific to the Pipelle device by direct
full-text verification (22 of 166 attempts, 13.3%).^1-3^ After a failed
office attempt, we modeled two pathways rather than assuming universal
escalation to D&C: a repeat office attempt, estimated to occur in 5% of
failures based on a Pipelle decision-tree model's expert clinical
estimate,^12^ succeeding 75% of the time based on a separate, much larger
cohort of patients with an insufficient endometrial sample, among whom a
second sampling attempt was adequate in three-quarters of those who
underwent one,^15^ or direct escalation to D&C. The
combined-arm probability of escalation to D&C was the directly observed rate
from a 10.5-year, 111-visit combined-screening cohort (2 of 111 visits,
1.8%).^4^ The combined arm's incremental procedure time (median 5 minutes,
range 1-12 minutes) and incremental anesthesia requirement (no increase in
dosing) were drawn from a prospective feasibility study of the combined
procedure.^5^

We conducted five complementary sensitivity analyses. First, deterministic
one-way sensitivity analysis varied each of ten parameters individually
across its low/high bound while holding all others at base case. Second,
probabilistic sensitivity analysis drew 1,000 Monte Carlo samples, with each
parameter sampled from a distribution matched to its evidence type (beta for
probabilities, gamma for costs, triangular for parameters whose uncertainty
is a structural or plausibility range rather than a formal confidence
interval). Third, threshold analysis solved for the parameter value at which
the combined strategy's cost advantage over office biopsy would be lost.
Fourth, scenario analysis modeled illustrative Medicaid and commercial
reimbursement and an alternative structural assumption about the combined
arm's preoperative visit. Fifth, budget-impact analysis projected annualized
savings across illustrative cohort sizes.

To test whether the base-case conclusion depends on national-average
Medicare pricing, we re-priced all three strategies at four localities: the
national average, a mid-cost state, a low-cost locality, and a high-cost
locality. Professional-fee components were adjusted using the Medicare
Geographic Practice Cost Index for the relevant procedure code and setting,
applying the standard relative-value formula (work relative-value units x
work index + practice-expense relative-value units x practice-expense index
+ malpractice relative-value units x malpractice index, divided by the
unadjusted total).^6^ The D&C facility fee was adjusted using the real
Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System wage index for the relevant
core-based statistical area,^7^ applying the labor-related-share formula
(labor share x wage index + [1 - labor share]) with the actual 60%
labor-related share finalized for the payment year.^8^ This geographic
analysis was kept deterministic rather than folded into the probabilistic
sensitivity analysis, since geographic variation is a question of whether
the conclusion generalizes to a different practice location rather than a
source of parameter uncertainty.

We conducted two clinical-outcome sensitivity analyses, computed from the
same probabilistic-sensitivity draws as the cost outputs. First, we
estimated each strategy's exposure to D&C-related adverse events (a
composite of uterine perforation, cervical false passage, and severe
hemorrhage, pooled from a cohort of 5,359 nonobstetric D&Cs)^9^ as a
function of that strategy's probability of ultimately requiring D&C, either
as the primary procedure or as a rescue procedure after a failed sampling
attempt. Second, we estimated each arm's probability of a failed sampling
attempt going undiagnosed for cancer or precancer, combined with the
probability of cancer or precancer among women with a failed or insufficient
sample, drawn from a general (non-Lynch) postmenopausal-bleeding
meta-analysis.^10^ Under the repeat-attempt-or-D&C structure described
above, the office arm's failed attempts are accounted for entirely by
either a successful repeat or escalation to D&C, leaving no probability
mass for a sample that is neither adequately resampled nor escalated; the
combined arm's directly observed escalation rate similarly accounts for
essentially all combined-biopsy failures. Neither arm therefore retained an
estimable undiagnosed-failure probability under current evidence; this null
result, and what it does and does not imply, is addressed in the
Discussion.

As a separate, deterministic check on the same equivalent-effectiveness
assumption, we also computed each strategy's overall probability of
detecting a true cancer or endometrial hyperplasia, combining each arm's
sampling-escalation probabilities with published Pipelle and D&C
sensitivities from a general (non-Lynch) diagnostic-accuracy
meta-analysis.^17^ This calculation is a point estimate only, not
integrated into the probabilistic sensitivity analysis; see Discussion for
its limitations.

The geographic sensitivity analysis characterizes setting-level
heterogeneity (how the base-case conclusion varies by practice location);
it does not characterize patient-level heterogeneity, which was not
modeled -- the model does not stratify results by age, genotype,
menopausal status, or other individual patient characteristics.
Distributional or equity effects (e.g., differential access or affordability
across patient subgroups) were outside this analysis's scope. Structural
modeling assumptions describing actual clinical workflow (e.g., whether the
combined-biopsy strategy requires a separate preoperative office visit)
were informed by clinician-investigator practice experience; no formal
patient or public engagement process was undertaken in developing this
model.

We compared the model's cost estimates against three independently
published analyses as a validation check: a historical office-biopsy cost
anchor,^11^ a Medicare-payer-perspective decision-tree comparing Pipelle
sampling and D&C,^12^ and an independent U.S. economic model of office
versus institutional hysteroscopic surgery.^13^

All analyses were implemented in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing,
Vienna, Austria) and are publicly available, with every model parameter
individually cited to its source. [Author: confirm final phrasing for a
double-anonymized submission -- the public repository URL and any
institution-identifying detail belong on the title page, not here.] This
study is reported in accordance with the Consolidated Health Economic
Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS) 2022 statement; the completed
checklist is provided as Supplemental Digital Content.

## Results

In the base case, combined biopsy cost an estimated $506.11 per patient,
compared with $749.18 for standalone office biopsy and $3,839.81 for
operative D&C. Combined biopsy was $243.06 (32.4%) less expensive than
office biopsy, and both office-based strategies were substantially less
expensive than D&C, which was more costly than both alternatives at every
facility fee tested, including a facility fee of $0.

The combined-vs-office cost difference was most sensitive to the office
biopsy failure probability (range -$131.80 to -$491.54 across its 10.3%-20.0%
bound) and the combined arm's incremental procedure time (range -$376.80 to
-$9.01 across its observed 1-12 minute range). At the upper end of the
observed time range, the combined arm's advantage over office biopsy
narrowed to $9.01 but did not reverse.

Across 1,000 probabilistic-sensitivity draws, combined biopsy had a mean
cost of $539.93 (SD $116.01) and office biopsy a mean cost of $755.70 (SD
$119.99). Combined biopsy was the least expensive strategy in 91.4% of
draws; D&C was never the least expensive strategy in any draw. Combined
biopsy remained the least expensive strategy as long as the incremental
colonoscopy-suite time stayed below approximately 12.3 minutes and as long
as the office biopsy failure probability stayed above approximately 6.7%.
At illustrative cohort sizes of 10 to 1,000 patients screened annually,
adopting combined biopsy over standalone office biopsy was projected to
save $2,431 to $243,062 per year.

Combined biopsy remained the least expensive strategy in all four localities
tested. Its advantage over office biopsy ranged from $195.62 per patient in
the low-cost locality to $257.82 in the mid-cost locality to $333.44 per
patient in the high-cost locality -- that is, the combined-arm cost
advantage widened, rather than narrowed or reversed, at the high-cost
extreme.

D&C-rescue-driven major-adverse-event exposure was substantially lower for
combined biopsy (mean 0.36 events per 1,000 patients) than for office
biopsy (mean 2.48 per 1,000), reflecting the combined arm's lower
probability of ultimately requiring D&C. D&C itself carried a mean
adverse-event exposure of 19.19 per 1,000. Neither arm retained an
estimable delayed-neoplasia risk (a failed sample that is neither
adequately resampled nor rescued to D&C, and that represents cancer or
precancer): both the office-biopsy arm's repeat-attempt-or-D&C pathway and
the combined-biopsy arm's directly observed escalation rate accounted for
essentially all failed samples across all 1,000 draws, leaving 0.00
delayed-neoplasia probability for both strategies. This is a null result
under current evidence, not a finding that either strategy's true risk is
zero (see Discussion).

The secondary detection-probability check found each strategy's overall
probability of detecting a true cancer was 78.8% for office biopsy, 77.6%
for combined biopsy, and 88.0% for D&C; for atypical endometrial
hyperplasia, the corresponding probabilities were 74.8%, 74.1%, and 80.0%.
D&C's point estimate was the highest of the three for both conditions, but
its underlying sensitivity carries a very wide 95% confidence interval
(28.1%-99.3%, from only 5 pooled studies), compared with 56.5%-90.0% for
Pipelle; this ordering is therefore far from established (see Discussion).

## Discussion

<!-- DRAFT -- clinical/policy framing is a reasonable first pass, not
confirmed by the author. Written to satisfy the journal's explicit
instruction against "further research is needed" language: limitations are
paired with what specific evidence would resolve each one, not a generic
closing line. -->

In this decision-analytic cost-minimization model, endometrial biopsy
performed during an already-scheduled surveillance colonoscopy cost
substantially less than either standalone office biopsy or operative D&C
for Lynch syndrome surveillance, and this advantage held across
deterministic and probabilistic parameter uncertainty, four Medicare payment
localities spanning a national low-cost to high-cost range, and illustrative
payer-mix and structural scenarios. The combined strategy also carried
substantially lower exposure to D&C-related adverse events than standalone
office biopsy, because fewer combined-biopsy patients ultimately require a
D&C rescue procedure. Together, these findings suggest combined biopsy is
not simply a lower-cost substitute but a strategy that reduces both cost and
a specific, quantifiable procedural risk relative to standalone office
biopsy -- a combination that should make it an attractive default where
gastroenterology and gynecology scheduling can be coordinated.

This model's principal limitation is that its cost-minimization design
formally assumes equivalent diagnostic effectiveness across strategies. We
tested that assumption two ways, with different results. First, whether a
failed sample goes entirely undiagnosed: both arms' failure-resolution
pathways -- the office arm's repeat-attempt-or-D&C structure and the
combined arm's directly observed escalation rate -- account for essentially
all failed attempts, leaving no probability mass for a sample that is
neither resampled nor escalated to D&C. This is a genuine absence of
evidence for a differential risk, not evidence the risks are equal: none of
the underlying studies was designed to detect a distinct unresolved-failure
outcome, so a real difference could exist without being visible here.
Second, each strategy's overall detection probability for a true cancer or
precancer, combining escalation probabilities with published (non-Lynch)
Pipelle and D&C sensitivities, suggested D&C's point estimate exceeds
office and combined biopsy's (see Results) -- but D&C's own sensitivity
carries a 95% confidence interval spanning 28.1%-99.3%, so this difference
is far from established. What would resolve either test is a study that
follows sampling failures and their eventual diagnoses forward in a
Lynch-specific population, rather than inferring effectiveness from
general-population sensitivities or aggregate escalation rates.

Other limitations warrant explicit statement. The office arm's
repeat-attempt structure rests on a non-Lynch evidence base: the 5%
repeat-attempt probability is an expert clinical estimate from a Pipelle
decision-tree model, and the 75% repeat-attempt success probability comes
from a 1,120-patient insufficient-endometrial-sample cohort with a
reconstructed, not primary-reported, confidence interval. Both parameters'
effects were tested in sensitivity analysis rather than treated as fixed,
but neither is a direct measurement in a Lynch surveillance population.
Operative D&C's own risk
of an inadequate specimen was not modeled, so its cost is likely a
conservative (lower-bound) estimate relative to a strategy that sometimes
requires its own repeat procedure. The base-case D&C cost partially
monetizes adverse-event risk: it includes an expected cost for uterine
perforation managed by diagnostic laparoscopy, the only management
pathway with a cost fully traceable to current Medicare payment data --
a deliberate lower bound. Perforations requiring laparotomy, a
substantial minority of cases, could not be costed: the relevant
procedure code is inpatient-only under Medicare, with no outpatient
facility rate. Severe hemorrhage was not monetized at all, since no
source described its management pathway without relying on a clinically
unrelated economic model, which we avoided. The per-1,000 adverse-event
and delayed-neoplasia exposures reported above remain unmonetized
clinical counts, not cost inputs. Finally, several
inputs -- the diagnostic sensitivity values underlying the detection-probability
analysis above, and the D&C and hysteroscopy adverse-event
probabilities -- are drawn from general, non-Lynch populations rather than
from women undergoing Lynch syndrome surveillance specifically, because
Lynch-specific data for these particular parameters were not identified in
the literature search underlying this model.

These findings are consistent with a broader literature showing that
office-based procedures generally cost health systems less than the same or
related procedures performed in an institutional setting, and that adding a
brief procedure to an already-sedated encounter avoids much of the
incremental cost of a separate procedural visit. Our model extends this
general pattern to the specific, three-way comparison relevant to Lynch
syndrome surveillance and quantifies it using contemporary, publicly
documented Medicare payment data rather than modeled charges.

Endometrial biopsy performed during an already-scheduled surveillance
colonoscopy costs less, and exposes patients to less D&C-related procedural
risk, than either standalone office biopsy or operative D&C for Lynch
syndrome surveillance. This conclusion was robust to parameter uncertainty
and practice location in every sensitivity analysis performed. Programs
that can coordinate gastroenterology and gynecology scheduling should
consider combined biopsy as the default surveillance strategy for this
population.

manuscript -- was wired into `analysis/13_diagnostic_yield.R` and reported

Pipelle and conventional D&C match exactly what was already coded into
`R/diagnostic_yield.R` (added in an earlier session), confirming that
earlier code comment's "verified directly from the full text" claim
independently rather than trusting it as-is.

**Table 1.** Model parameters: base-case value, low/high bound, distribution,
source citation, and evidence tier for every parameter in the model.
Satisfies CHEERS items 16 and 18 (a table of all assumptions with
justification and range). *Source:* `tables/manuscript_table1_parameters.csv`.

**Table 2.** Base-case cost and clinical-outcome summary: initial cost,
escalation probability, expected total cost, and mean PSA-derived
adverse-event and delayed-neoplasia exposure, by strategy. *Source:*
`tables/manuscript_table10_summary.csv` (built by
`analysis/11_manuscript_table10_summary.R` from the same PSA draws the
Results text is based on).

**Figure 1.** Decision-tree model diagram: the three strategies, their
chance-node escalation probabilities, and the path-specific and
expected total cost at each terminal node. Satisfies CHEERS item 15 (a
figure summarizing the model). *Source:* `figures/figure7_decision_tree.png`
(built by `analysis/10_decision_tree_figure.R` directly from live model
output, not hand-drawn).

**Figure 2.** Probabilistic sensitivity analysis: distribution of the
incremental cost of combined biopsy versus office biopsy across 1,000 Monte
Carlo draws. *Source:* `figures/figure4_psa_incremental_cost.jpeg`.

**Figure 3.** Geographic sensitivity analysis: expected cost per strategy
at four localities (national, Colorado, low-cost, high-cost). *Source:*
`figures/figure6_geographic_sensitivity.jpeg`.
